title: HNSW indexing in vector databases
text:
A vector database stores embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour queries. Scanning every vector is exact but becomes slow as the collection grows, so most systems use an approximate index. Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, usually shortened to HNSW, are the most common choice. An HNSW index arranges vectors in several layers. The top layer is sparse and lets a search jump quickly across the whole space, while lower layers are denser and refine the result until the bottom layer contains every vector.

Two parameters shape the index. The parameter m controls how many links each node keeps to its neighbours; a larger m improves recall and uses more memory. The parameter ef_construct controls how many candidates are examined while the graph is being built; a larger value produces a better graph but makes indexing slower. At query time a third parameter, ef or hnsw_ef, sets how many candidates are explored. Raising it improves recall at the cost of latency.

Qdrant implements HNSW and combines it with payload filtering. A filter such as setup_id equals naive-500-100 restricts results to points whose payload matches. Because filtering during graph traversal can disconnect the graph, Qdrant builds extra links for indexed payload fields so that filtered searches stay accurate. For this reason, fields used often in filters, such as setup_id or run_id, should have a payload index.

Memory is the main operational concern. Vectors, graph links and payloads all consume RAM unless they are moved to disk. Quantization reduces vector size, for example by storing each float as a single byte, with a small loss of precision. Many teams keep original vectors on disk and use quantized copies for the first pass, then rescore the best candidates with the original vectors.

When comparing RAG experiments, remember that approximate search adds its own noise. If two setups differ by a fraction of a percent in recall, the difference may come from index parameters and not from chunking or embeddings. Fix the HNSW settings across a comparison, or measure against an exact brute-force search first to know the ceiling.

title: Chunking strategies for retrieval
text:
Chunking is the step that splits a document into passages that can be embedded and retrieved. The choice affects every later stage because the chunk is the unit that gets a vector, a score and a place in the final context.

The simplest strategy is the fixed token window. The text is cut every N tokens, optionally with an overlap of M tokens so that a sentence near a boundary appears in two neighbouring chunks. A window of 100 tokens with no overlap is a minimal baseline. It is cheap and deterministic, but it often cuts sentences in half and separates a statement from the sentence that explains it. A window of 500 tokens with an overlap of 100 keeps more context, but each chunk now covers several ideas, so its embedding becomes an average of them and may match a specific question less sharply.

Recursive splitting tries a list of separators in order, for example blank lines, then newlines, then sentence endings, then spaces. It keeps paragraphs together when they fit and only falls back to smaller units when needed. Document-aware splitting goes further and follows headings, list items or code blocks, which works well for Markdown and technical manuals. Semantic chunking embeds sentences and starts a new chunk where the similarity between neighbours drops, which tries to place boundaries where the topic changes, at the price of an extra embedding pass during ingestion.

Small chunks give precise matches but lose context. Large chunks keep context but dilute the signal and use more of the language model's context window. There is no universal best size; it depends on the corpus, the embedding model's maximum input and the kind of questions. That is why chunking should be a named, recorded profile and not a hard-coded constant.

Whatever the strategy, every chunk needs a stable identity and a reference back to the source, such as document ID and character offsets. Deterministic chunk IDs allow re-ingestion to overwrite instead of duplicate, and offsets allow evaluation against labelled answer spans. A question whose answer straddles a boundary is a useful test: a no-overlap window may retrieve neither half, while an overlapping window or a larger one will find it.

title: Late chunking
text:
Late chunking is an alternative to splitting a document before embedding it. In the usual pipeline each chunk is embedded on its own, so the model never sees the text around it. A sentence such as it was founded in 1998 becomes ambiguous once the earlier sentence naming the company is in a different chunk, because the pronoun no longer has an antecedent.

Late chunking reverses the order of the steps. The whole document, or as much of it as the model can accept, is passed through a long-context embedding model first. The model produces one contextual vector per token, and each token's vector already reflects the surrounding text. Only afterwards are the token vectors grouped according to the chunk boundaries and pooled, usually by averaging, into one embedding per chunk. The boundaries decide how the vectors are grouped, but they no longer limit what the model could see.

The approach depends on the embedding model. It needs a model that returns token-level outputs and supports long inputs, since a model limited to a few hundred tokens would gain little. The model name and revision, the maximum input length, the pooling method and the boundary rule all belong in the setup definition, otherwise the results cannot be reproduced.

The expected benefit is greatest for documents full of references: pronouns, abbreviations, and sections that depend on earlier definitions. The expected cost is more compute at indexing time and a hard dependency on one family of models. Documents longer than the model's window must be split into large overlapping segments first, which brings back a smaller version of the boundary problem.

In an experiment, late chunking should be compared against naive windows using the same corpus, the same boundaries and the same questions. Questions that contain no ambiguous reference are unlikely to show a difference; questions that need a nearby sentence to be understood are where a gain should appear.

title: Hybrid search with BM25 and dense vectors
text:
Dense retrieval compares the meaning of a query and a passage through embeddings. Lexical retrieval compares the words themselves. BM25 is the standard lexical scoring function: it rewards passages that contain the query terms, weights rare terms more heavily than common ones through inverse document frequency, and dampens the effect of repeating a term many times and of very long passages.

The two approaches fail in different ways. A dense model handles paraphrases well, so how do plants make food from light can find a passage about photosynthesis even without shared words. The same model can miss exact strings such as product codes, error identifiers, person names or rare technical terms, because their embeddings are not very distinctive. BM25 finds such a code immediately but returns nothing useful when the question and the answer use different vocabulary.

Hybrid search runs both and merges the two ranked lists. A common fusion method is Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Each passage receives a score of one divided by a constant plus its rank in each list, and the scores are added. It only uses ranks, so the incompatible score scales of BM25 and cosine similarity do not matter. A constant of 60 is the traditional default. Another option is a weighted sum of normalized scores, which gives direct control over the balance but requires careful normalization.

In Qdrant, a sparse vector can be stored next to the dense vector in the same point, and a query can prefetch candidates from each and then fuse them. Sparse vectors may come from BM25-style term weights or from a learned sparse model.

Hybrid search is an experiment dimension, not an automatic default. The setup should record the sparse method, the number of candidates taken from each list, the fusion algorithm and its weights. To see the effect, the test set needs both kinds of query: paraphrased questions where dense retrieval should win, and exact-identifier questions where lexical retrieval should win.

title: Embedding models and dimensions
text:
An embedding model maps text to a vector of fixed length. Texts with similar meaning should land close together under a distance measure, usually cosine similarity or the dot product. The vector length, called the dimension, is fixed by the model. The model nomic-embed-text produces 768 dimensions, while many other models produce 384, 1024 or 3072.

A collection in a vector database is created with one dimension and one distance metric. Vectors from different models cannot be compared, even if the dimensions happen to be equal, because each model defines its own space. Switching models therefore means re-embedding the whole corpus into a new collection. For the same reason, the query must be embedded with exactly the model that embedded the documents.

Some models expect an instruction prefix. A retrieval model may be trained to see search_query: before a question and search_document: before a passage, and its quality drops if the prefixes are omitted. The prefix is part of the configuration and should be recorded with the model name and revision.

Every model has a maximum input length measured in tokens. Text beyond the limit is silently truncated by some servers, which means a very large chunk may be embedded from only its beginning. Chunk sizes should stay safely under that limit.

Ollama serves embedding models locally and exposes them over a simple HTTP API on port 11434. Requests can carry several texts at once, so a batch size setting, such as 32 chunks per request, trades memory for throughput. Timeouts and a small number of retries protect a long ingestion run from a temporary failure.

Larger dimensions can capture more nuance but cost more storage and make search slower. Some models support truncating the vector to a shorter length with a modest loss of quality, a technique often called Matryoshka representation. If dimensions are shortened, that choice must be written into the setup, because the collection's configured size has to match.

title: Reranking retrieved passages
text:
The first stage of retrieval has to be fast, so it compares a query with millions of precomputed vectors. A bi-encoder embeds the query and the passages independently, and the comparison is a cheap vector operation. The independence is what makes it fast and also what limits its accuracy: the model never sees the query and the passage together.

A reranker is a second stage that fixes this. A cross-encoder reads the query and a candidate passage as one input and outputs a relevance score. Because it can compare individual words and their relations across the pair, it is usually much more accurate than vector similarity. It is also far too slow to run over the whole collection, so it is applied only to the top candidates from the first stage, perhaps the best 50 or 100, and the result is cut down to the final handful of passages.

The design involves a trade-off between recall and latency. The first stage must have a high enough recall at the candidate depth, since a passage that is not retrieved cannot be rescued by the reranker. Increasing the number of candidates raises the chance of including the right passage and increases reranking time linearly.

Rerankers also interact with chunking. Small chunks give the model little text to judge, while very large chunks may exceed its input length. When neighbouring chunks of the same document both appear in the results, a merge policy can combine adjacent hits into one longer passage before they are passed to the language model.

In an experiment the reranker model, its version, the candidate depth and the final cut-off are all part of the setup. Measure the gain by comparing the same first-stage run with and without reranking, on the same questions, and watch the latency numbers as well as the ranking metrics.

title: The first ascent of Mount Everest
text:
Mount Everest, on the border between Nepal and Tibet, is the highest mountain above sea level. Its summit is about 8,849 metres high. The Nepalese name is Sagarmatha and the Tibetan name is Chomolungma. The mountain was named after Sir George Everest, a British surveyor general of India, in the 1850s, after the Great Trigonometrical Survey had calculated its height.

Several expeditions tried to climb it before success came. In the 1920s British teams explored the northern approach from Tibet. In 1924 George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared high on the mountain while attempting the summit, and it has never been settled whether they reached the top. Mallory's body was found in 1999.

The first confirmed ascent took place on 29 May 1953. Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer from Nepal, reached the summit as part of a British expedition led by John Hunt. The expedition was large and carefully organised. It used supplementary oxygen, a chain of camps and many porters, and the final camp was established high on the south-east ridge. Hillary and Tenzing climbed the last stretch from this camp, including a rock step that is now named the Hillary Step, although the feature is reported to have changed after the 2015 earthquake.

After 1953 the mountain became a target for many nations. Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler made the first ascent without supplementary oxygen in 1978, and Messner climbed it solo two years later. Over the decades the number of climbers has grown to several hundred in a good season, which has led to queues near the summit, concerns about waste, and debate about how the Sherpa community, whose guides and porters carry the greatest share of the risk, should be supported and compensated.

title: Brewing better filter coffee
text:
Good filter coffee depends on a few variables that can be measured: the ratio of coffee to water, the grind size, the water temperature, the contact time and the freshness of the beans. Changing one at a time makes it easy to taste what each does.

A common starting ratio is 60 grams of coffee per litre of water, which is about 1 to 16.7. For a single large cup of 300 millilitres that means 18 grams of ground coffee. Weighing both coffee and water is more reliable than using scoops, because beans differ in density.

Grind size controls the speed of extraction. Too fine a grind slows the flow and pulls out bitter, harsh compounds, so the cup tastes over-extracted. Too coarse a grind lets water pass quickly and the cup tastes sour and thin, which is a sign of under-extraction. For a pour-over cone, a medium grind similar to coarse sand is a good beginning. Adjust it in small steps if the brew takes much longer than about three minutes or finishes much sooner than two and a half.

Water should be hot but not boiling, between 92 and 96 degrees Celsius. Boiling water can scorch delicate light roasts, while lower temperatures suit dark roasts that extract easily. Pour a small amount first, roughly twice the weight of the coffee, and wait 30 to 45 seconds. This bloom releases carbon dioxide from freshly roasted beans, which would otherwise push water away from the grounds. Then add the rest in slow circles.

Beans are best used within a few weeks of the roast date and ground just before brewing, because ground coffee loses aroma within minutes. Store them in an airtight container away from light, heat and moisture. Use filtered water if the tap water is very hard, since minerals affect both taste and the build-up of scale in the kettle.

title: Service error codes reference
text:
This reference lists the error codes returned by the Orders API, version 2.3. Each code has a stable identifier, an HTTP status, and a recommended action.

ERR_4001 means the request body is not valid JSON. The HTTP status is 400. Check the Content-Type header and the syntax of the body.

ERR_4012 means the authentication token has expired. The HTTP status is 401. Request a new token from the /auth/refresh endpoint and repeat the call. Tokens are valid for 3600 seconds.

ERR_4034 means the account is not allowed to modify orders in the state CANCELLED. The HTTP status is 403. Cancelled orders are read-only; create a new order instead.

ERR_4045 means the order with the supplied order_id was not found. The HTTP status is 404. Verify the identifier and the environment, since sandbox and production orders are stored separately.

ERR_4091 means a concurrent update conflict. The HTTP status is 409. Another request changed the order after it was read. Fetch the order again, apply the change to the new version and send the update with the new version number in the If-Match header.

ERR_4290 means the rate limit was exceeded. The HTTP status is 429. The default limit is 100 requests per minute per API key. The Retry-After header contains the number of seconds to wait. Clients should use exponential backoff with jitter.

ERR_5003 means the payment provider did not respond in time. The HTTP status is 503. The order is left in the state PENDING_PAYMENT and the call can be repeated safely with the same Idempotency-Key header.

Unknown codes starting with ERR_5 indicate a server-side problem. Include the value of the X-Request-Id response header when contacting support, because it allows the request to be found in the logs.

title: How plants turn light into food
text:
Plants, algae and some bacteria make their own food by capturing energy from sunlight. The process is called photosynthesis, and it is the basis of nearly every food chain on Earth. It also produces the oxygen that most living things breathe.

In plants the work happens mainly in the leaves, inside small structures called chloroplasts. The chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, the green pigment that absorbs light, mostly in the red and blue parts of the spectrum and reflects green, which is why leaves look green. Water is taken up by the roots and travels to the leaves through vessels in the stem. Carbon dioxide enters the leaf from the air through tiny pores called stomata, which open and close to control water loss.

Photosynthesis has two linked stages. In the light-dependent reactions, which take place in the membranes inside the chloroplast, the energy of light is used to split water molecules. This releases oxygen and produces two energy-carrying molecules, ATP and NADPH. In the second stage, called the Calvin cycle, the plant uses that stored energy to attach carbon from carbon dioxide to existing molecules and build sugars, such as glucose. The sugars are used immediately for growth and respiration, converted to starch for storage, or transported to other parts of the plant.

The overall reaction can be summarised as six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water, with light energy, giving one molecule of glucose and six of oxygen.

The rate depends on light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. When light is weak, the rate is limited by light. When light is strong, another factor, such as carbon dioxide or the temperature-sensitive enzymes, becomes the limit. Gardeners and greenhouse growers use these relationships when they adjust lighting, ventilation and heating to improve crop yields.
